sections.heading: Asking God to wake me up
sections.text: Father, wake me up. I have been drifting through life as if I were dreaming, chasing things that cannot hold me or save me. Help me stop long enough to look honestly at myself—where I am going, what I am becoming, and how soon I will stand before you. Do not let me keep living distracted from the truth.
theological_themes: Spiritual awakening from distraction and vanity

scripture_references.connection: Ecclesiastes calls people to remember their Creator before weakness and death expose the emptiness of a life lived without God. That directly supports the prayer’s movement from distraction to sober self-examination.
This passage grounds the prayer’s awareness that life is temporary and that each person must finally answer to God. It gives biblical weight to the request to look forward honestly.

sections.heading: Remembering that I belong to you
sections.text: You made me. Everything I have—my body, my mind, my life, my breath—comes from you. I live in this body for a little while, like a traveler in a tent, and I am not here by accident. Since I was made by you and for you, teach me to want your ways and not just my own.
theological_themes: God as Creator and giver of life
Life as temporary stewardship before God

scripture_references.connection: Paul teaches that God made the world, gives life and breath to all, and is the one in whom human beings live. This supports the prayer’s confession that life is received from God and should be directed toward him.
Paul uses the image of the body as a tent to describe the temporary nature of earthly life. That illuminates the prayer’s concrete sense of living briefly in a body entrusted by God.

sections.heading: Confessing how I have ignored you
sections.text: God, you have been good to me, and I have treated you as if you were small, distant, or optional. When I think about your greatness and your kindness, I am ashamed of how numb I have been. I have sinned foolishly. I have pushed you out of my thoughts. I have failed to treat knowing you as the purpose of my life. I have not taken seriously the need of my own heart.
theological_themes: Neglect of God as the true purpose of life
Humility and shame over spiritual insensitivity

scripture_references.connection: Romans describes the sinful exchange of honoring God for serving created things. It gives biblical shape to the prayer’s confession of ignoring God’s greatness and chasing lesser things.
This psalm names the practical godlessness of a heart that does not have room for God in its thoughts. It supports the prayer’s confession that God has been neglected inwardly, not merely outwardly.

sections.heading: Coming before you without delay
sections.text: Even now my mind feels pulled in different directions, and my heart is crooked. Still, underneath all the confusion, I know I need you and I want to come home to you. Do not let me put this off. Break the spell that my sinful desires have had over me. Free me from the things that keep dragging me away from you, and bring me into the settled joy of resting in you. You made me; please do not leave me to myself.
theological_themes: God’s gracious drawing of a divided heart

scripture_references.connection: James calls divided sinners to turn back to God with humility, repentance, and nearness to him. This closely matches the prayer’s urgency not to delay coming to God.
Jesus promises that those who come to him will not be cast out. This supports the prayer’s hope that the sinner may come honestly and urgently to God rather than despairing.

Paul describes the painful conflict of a person who sees the good yet feels the pull of sin, and he points to deliverance through Jesus Christ. That helps frame the prayer’s divided mind and desire for rescue.

sections.heading: Asking the Spirit to teach me Christ
sections.text: Holy Spirit, teach me what I most need to learn about Christ. I am slow, stubborn, and easily confused. Show me the truth that gives life. Bring my heart to Jesus, not just my ideas. And Father, please listen to these broken prayers, even when I do not know how to say them well.
theological_themes: The Holy Spirit’s work of teaching and leading to Christ
Dependence on grace for spiritual understanding

scripture_references.connection: Jesus says the Spirit will guide his people into truth and glorify Christ by making known what belongs to him. This directly grounds the request for the Spirit to teach the life-giving lessons of Christ.
Paul teaches that the things of God are understood by the Spirit rather than by natural human ability. This supports the prayer’s admission of slowness and need for divine teaching.
Romans describes the Spirit helping believers in weakness when they do not know how to pray as they ought. This fits the closing request that God hear broken cries.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original calls God an “injured” benefactor. I rendered this as sinning against and dishonoring God’s goodness, while avoiding the implication that God is vulnerable or diminished in his divine being.

The phrase “fatal enchantment” could sound like literal magic in contemporary English. I preserved its force as the captivating, enslaving power of sinful desires without introducing an occult framework.
The original’s appeal that God “made me and canst not forget me” was kept as a plea for mercy based on creaturely dependence, not as a claim that creation alone guarantees salvation.
significant_interpretive_choices: The opening address to the soul was recast as a direct request to the Father to awaken the speaker, preserving the inward self-exhortation while keeping the whole prayer naturally addressed to God.
“Look inward, forward, upward” was interpreted as self-examination, awareness of death and judgment, and turning to God, rather than as a general mindfulness exercise.

“My secret dispositions still desire thee” was rendered as an awakened underlying need and desire for God amid confusion, not as a denial of the prayer’s strong confession of a perverse and divided nature.
“Vital lessons of Christ” was interpreted as the Spirit’s work of bringing the sinner to the living truth of Christ, not merely giving moral instruction.
